svg.aria-label: Diagram: how Classic VPN and HA VPN differ in Google Cloud, with Classic described by the documentation as the predecessor to HA VPN and HA VPN as replacing it; Classic having a single interface, a single external IP address, static policy-based or route-based routing only, a 99.9 percent SLA and no IPv6 support, known in the API as the target-vpn-gateway resource; HA VPN having two interfaces with two external IP addresses chosen automatically from unique pools, dynamic BGP routing only, a 99.99 percent SLA for most topologies, dual-stack and IPv6-only support, known as the vpn-gateway resource; the trap that an HA VPN gateway can be configured with only one active interface but then carries no availability SLA at all; the fact that per-tunnel bandwidth is identical for both at 250,000 packets per second, so HA VPN buys availability rather than throughput; that VPN tunnels must be created in pairs before traffic can pass; and the migration constraints, above all that leftover custom static routes from the old policy-based tunnels must be removed because static routes outrank dynamic ones
svg.title: Classic VPN versus HA VPN: the SLA is the headline, the leftover static routes are the hazard
svg.text: Two gateways, and the documentation is blunt about which one it expects you to use.
Classic is called the predecessor. HA VPN is said to replace it. Neither word is mine.
CLASSIC VPN
• ONE interface, ONE external IP address
• Static routing only: policy-based or
route-based
• SLA of 99.9% service availability
• Does NOT support IPv6
• External IPs AND forwarding rules
must be created by you
• API: target-vpn-gateway
• No two tunnels to the same peer gateway
HA VPN
• TWO interfaces, TWO external IPs chosen
automatically, each from a unique pool
• Dynamic routing only: BGP
• 99.99% SLA for most topologies
• Dual stack AND IPv6-only
• IPs come from a pool; NO forwarding
rules required
• API: vpn-gateway
• Each interface supports many tunnels
The configuration that looks like HA VPN and carries no SLA
You CAN configure an HA VPN gateway with only one active interface and one external IP
address — however, that configuration does NOT provide an availability SLA. Nothing warns you.
Per-tunnel bandwidth is identical. HA VPN buys availability, not throughput.
EACH Cloud VPN tunnel — either kind — supports up to 250,000 packets per second for the SUM
of ingress and egress. That is between 1 Gbps and 3 Gbps depending on packet size.
Measured in bytes, the 3-Gbps ceiling is 375 MBps. Compare Sent + Received against that.
A tunnel is half a connection
TWO tunnels must be established between two gateways — each defines the connection from its
own gateway’s point of view, and traffic passes only after the PAIR is up. Cloud VPN starts IKE.
Migrating is a rebuild, not a conversion
• The peer device MUST speak BGP. If it does not, you cannot use HA VPN at all.
• The gateway’s external IP address CANNOT be preserved. Two new ones are created.
• An existing tunnel cannot be migrated. Create new ones, then delete the old ones.
• You cannot connect a Classic gateway to an HA VPN gateway, so there is no half-way state.
• The Cloud Router must NOT already manage a BGP session for a Partner Interconnect attachment.
• REMOVE ANY LEFTOVER CUSTOM STATIC ROUTES from the old policy-based or route-based tunnels.
#84 is why this one bites: static routes ALWAYS outrank the dynamic routes you just built.
What the two documents each tell you
The comparison table lists Classic as static-only, and the only documented way to create a
Classic gateway is the static-routing page. Meanwhile the routing reference still describes
“a Classic VPN tunnel that uses dynamic routing” — behaviour, not a path you can newly take.
Read the table for what you can BUILD today; read the routing page for what EXISTS already.
